title: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt: Specs, Benchmarks and Size (2026)
summary: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt changes error rates, speed, and cost per model call. This helps you decide if it's worth testing for your automations.
body_markdown:
## Nemotron 3.5 Bolt was released by NVIDIA


NVIDIA published Nemotron 3.5 Bolt on Hugging Face under the model name NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-4GB, and the[model page](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-4GB) is the only source this article treats as settled. Anything the page doesn't state, such as benchmark claims or task fit, stays unverified here until you test it.


### What Nemotron 3.5 Bolt is


It's a model from NVIDIA's Nemotron family, and the repository name is one of several specs I take from the page for this section.


For an automation team, that means the useful questions are the ones a spec sheet answers: what input it accepts, what output it returns, and under what licence. Read the page for those, not a summary of it, including this one.


### Where to get Nemotron 3.5 Bolt weights


Getting the weights is the easy part, since they live on that Hugging Face page. Reaching the model from a workflow is the harder one, and it depends on whether your automation platform has a step that can call it.


### Getting an open-weight model into any automation tool


Whatever platform you use, the model has to answer over HTTP before a workflow can reach it. There are three ways to get there, and they work the same way in most tools.


The first is to serve the weights yourself. Ollama, llama.cpp and vLLM can each load a GGUF or a set of weights and expose an OpenAI-compatible HTTP endpoint.


Any platform with an HTTP request step or a custom-model step can then call that endpoint like any other API. The cost is that you run and maintain the server.


The second is to use a hosted provider that lists the model. Check the provider's catalogue for the exact model name, since a similar-sounding model is not the same one. If it is there, you get an API key and an endpoint without running hardware.


The third is to check whether your platform accepts a custom base URL for its AI or OpenAI-style step. If it does, you can point it at either of the first two options and keep the platform's own model step.


If it doesn't, the plain HTTP step is the fallback.


Each route ends in the same place, an endpoint that accepts a request and returns a completion. Until one exists, no workflow tool can use Bolt, however good its connector list looks.


[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/) runs the model you already chose on your own provider key, so spend lands on your provider account, and MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run it in production.


Its "pick Bolt from the list" step only works once an endpoint like the ones above exists and your provider entry points at it.


502 integrations is what the library below lists, as connector libraries advertise big catalogues. Most of those are Gmail-style app connectors, so the count says nothing about whether an integration accepts a model endpoint. The filter sidebar's Artificial Intelligence category is the part that counts.


Check that category for the provider you need before you plan a test.
